newsitem.title: USA: Software, electronic games aimed at girls.
newsitem.headline: Software, electronic games aimed at girls.

text.p: Forget it, girls. You don't really want to be a pretend astronaut, firefighter or space-age warrior. You're too busy arranging your dates, talking on the phone and perfecting your makeup. Right?
This is the message being sent to today's girls by several major toy manufacturers, who have developed computer games or electronic toys aimed at preteens and early teenagers.
Video and electronic toys are the fastest-growing segments of the over $20 billion U.S. toy industry, with video games last year surging ahead after a two year decline.

"Traditional toys, like classic and action games ... are forging new territory for the toy industry by incorporating classic hits with technological components," said George Volanakis, chairman of Toy Manufacturers of America Inc., the toy trade group, at the recent American International Toy Fair in New York.

Manufacturers have discovered a large, untapped market for computer and electronic toys -- girls -- and new products that will be in stores later this year address activities the companies feel the girls can't live without.

Computers have made it into Barbie-land. Following last year's Barbie fashion designer CD-ROM, Mattel Inc. has developed "Barbie Magic Hair Styler." The CD-ROM allows girls to cut, curl, brush, style and colour Barbie's hair on a computer screen. Barbie's makeup can also be changed endless times.

Barbie also has the "Ocean Discovery CD-ROM," where Barbie and her marine friends search for sunken treasure. For future society hostesses, Barbie has the "Make A Party" CD-ROM, where girls can plan, make and host a Barbie-themed celebration for their human and doll friends.
The CD-ROMs, which run on Windows 95, cost about $35 and will be available in the fall.

Barbie speaks in "Talk With Me Barbie." The doll can be hooked up to a computer, includes a CD-ROM and comes programmed to record and play back various information. By clicking on a computer screen, the doll can ask questions and discuss makeup, shopping, parties, careers, vacations or pets. The Talk With Me doll will cost about $90, will be available in October and will be advertised on television in November.
Hasbro Inc. has joined with Girl Tech Inc. to "empower girls to use technology and feel more comfortable with it," the toymaker said.

The 1997 line "focuses on keeping and sharing secrets," Hasbro said. These toys include "Swap-It Locket," where a girl uses a central recording unit and has two keys to "unlock" the messages so only she and her best friends can hear them ($14.99).

The "Me-Mail Message Center" ($18.99) allows girls to leave recorded messages or written statements on a dry-erase board, which can be put in a school locker or on a bedroom door. Friends can push a button to get outgoing messages.

"Snoopy Stopper Keepsakes Box" ($18.99) can be electronically programmed to keep nosy-bodies out and gives off an alarm when intruders try to open it. Similarly, the "Zap 'N Lock Journal" ($24.99) allows girls to use a remote control device to activate the "nosy-brother-proof" lock.
The toys are designed for girls age 6 and up and will be available in July.

For those girls who have more dates than they can handle, Tiger Electronics has developed "Dear Diary Really Dating Organiser." This electronic organiser, in girl-friendly colours of pink and lavender, has a romance indicator, slumber party game, pairing up-game and crush list. A secret password keeps information totally private. It is designed for girls 9 and up, costs $24.99 to $29.99, and will be available in April.

The "Dear Diary Clueless" organisers, after the movie and television show of the same name, help girls become and stay Betties -- that's Clueless-speak for beautiful girls. The organisers by Tiger either store general information or specialise in fashion and makeup information storage. They sell for $14.99 and up and will be available in April.

Girls also like to talk on the phone, and Tiger's "Clueless Hands Free Phone" is designed for that purpose. The working telephone, again in pink and purple, works like a regular phone but can be transformed into a hands-free version by detaching the earpiece and flexible microphone and attaching the base to a belt. It also comes programmed with the indespensible phrases, "as if," "whatever," and "I'm audi." There is a feature to alter voices and a security alert to detect evesdroppers who pick up an extension.
The phone will cost about $20 to $25 and will available in April.

Tyco Industries Inc., makers of such classics as View-Master and Matchbox cars, has Magic Date Ball, a takeoff on the Magic 8-Ball, which answered all of life's important questions. The Date Ball wants girls to ask, "Does he like me?," and "Will he ask me?" It sells for $21.99 and will be available in late summer.
